abstract: Offline retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices is updated through signed knowledge packs that carry text and precomputed embedding vectors. A signature proves who published a pack, not that its vectors encode its text. We study this text–vector integrity gap. A verifier that recomputes vectors and accepts them within a cosine tolerance concedes a predictable share of queries to an attacker who controls the vectors: the hijack rate equals the distribution of angular retrieval margins at the tolerance (the margin law). Margins are small in five corpora and two embedding models, so an idealised tolerance at the level of floating-point noise leaves up to 5.5% of queries exposed (at most 1.2% in any corpus once exact duplicate documents are excluded), and a threshold calibrated from our CPU INT8–FP32 comparison of a small embedding model (at the empirical 0.1% quantile of honest cosines) leaves 98–100% exposed; on a Raspberry Pi 5 running a local language model, such an attack lowers correct answers from 0.75 to 0.39. Integrity audits of compressed vector stores fare no better: on a FAISS product-quantisation index over 57,638 documents, tampered vectors that all pass the audit put the attacker’s document first for 25% of targets. Verifying quantisation codes instead, with ambiguity decided by the verifier, a calibrated guard band and canonicalisation, accepted every honest vector in our samples on three platforms and left the publisher no choice. We also show that common floating-point and dynamic-INT8 inference pipelines are not bit-reproducible across batch sizes or architectures, and report pre-registered negative results on abstention, context pruning and semantic screening. We release code and data.

sections.body:
The paper studies whether the precomputed vectors shipped in a signed knowledge pack encode the pack's text. Embedding a 950-passage pack on a Raspberry Pi 5 CPU took about 29 minutes in the earlier study, so packs ship vectors, and the signature covers them without binding them to the text.

The paper asks four questions: how many queries a tolerance-based check lets an attacker hijack (RQ1); how exposed compressed vector stores are (RQ2); whether exact verification closes the gap across hardware (RQ3); and what verification costs on the device's CPU end to end (RQ4). Experiments use a Raspberry Pi 5 running a local Qwen2.5-3B model, a desktop and an Apple laptop.

Contributions are the margin law, exposure measurements for tolerance checks and compressed stores, code-level verification, on-device cost, and pre-registered negative results.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Signatures prove who published a knowledge pack but not that its vectors encode its text, so the paper tests that gap.

sections.body:
The adversary is a compromised publisher, build pipeline, insider or store writer. Every text chunk passes content review, and the adversary chooses the vectors or codes. The adversary knows the public embedding model and may add chunks whose text passes review.

The paper compares five verifier designs: no verification (V0), signature only (V1), recomputation accepted within a cosine tolerance (V2), exact equality with a bit-reproducible computation (V3), and code-level verification for compressed stores (V4).

Out of scope are changes to model weights, chunk text, index structure beyond stored vectors or codes, the query channel, side channels and denial of service. Background reports that compression error is a fraction of a degree for SQ8 and tens of degrees for product and binary codes, so audits must tolerate it.
sections.heading: Background, Threat Model and Related Work
sections.headline: The threat model lets an attacker choose the vectors of review-admitted text, while verifiers recompute them or check exact codes.

sections.body:
For a query with gold unit g and closest competitor c, the angular margin m(q) is the competitor's angle to the query minus the gold unit's angle. An optimal attacker rotates the competitor towards the query by the tolerance angle, so rank 1 is hijacked exactly when the margin is below that angle. The hijack rate HR(τ) is the fraction of queries whose margin is below arccos τ. An operator can compute this rate from honest vectors and a query log, without attacking.

Stated limits: recomputation noise is ignored, small-tolerance exposure is an upper bound on harm, and on SQuAD the gold unit ranks first for 78% (BGE-M3) and 70% (MiniLM) of answerable questions.
sections.heading: The Margin Law
sections.headline: The margin law says an optimal attacker hijacks exactly the queries whose angular margin is below the tolerance angle, measurable without attacks.

sections.body:
Hardware is a Raspberry Pi 5 (16 GB, Arm Cortex-A76 CPU) running the language model, on-device embedding and the verifier on its CPU; a desktop (RTX 4090, 16 cores, WSL2) for artefacts and scale runs; and an Apple MacBook Air (16 GB) for cross-device code verification.

Models are Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (`Q4_K_M`) under llama.cpp, BGE-M3 dense retrieval, and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 in FP32 and dynamic INT8 under ONNX Runtime. Data are a 950-passage SQuAD 2.0 corpus with 300 questions, all 4,690 answerable development questions for scale, four BEIR corpora, and 1,000 MS MARCO v2.1 queries.

Hypotheses and decision gates were written before measurement but not deposited in a public registry. The protocol logs 34 deviation entries. Retrieval returns identical top-5 lists, and the earlier main configuration reproduces 60 of 60 answers exactly.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Experiments run on a Raspberry Pi 5, a desktop and an Apple laptop, with pinned models and a pre-registered protocol.

sections.body:
With FP32 cross-architecture noise as the tolerance, 0–5.5% of queries are exposed across the five corpora. Most exposure in ArguAna and NFCorpus comes from exact duplicate documents. At the MiniLM CPU INT8 reference threshold of 25.3 degrees, exposure is 98.7–100% in all five corpora.

For compressed stores, SQ8 leaves 2.0–14.5% of queries exposed and product quantisation 99.7–100%. On a FAISS product-quantisation index over 57,638 documents, tampered vectors that all pass the check rank the attacker's document first for 25% of targets.

On the Raspberry Pi, the attack under the INT8 reference threshold lowers correct answers from 0.75 to 0.39.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: At a float-noise tolerance 0–5.5% of queries stay hijackable, and at the INT8 reference threshold 98.7–100% do.

sections.body:
The discussion attributes tolerance failure to a mismatch of scales: retrieval decisions turn on small angular differences, with median margins of 2.1–7.4 degrees across five corpora and two models. Three deviation regimes are distinguished. FP32 cross-device noise is at most 0.04 degrees, but near-duplicate competitors keep up to 5.5% of queries exposed. INT8 inference, with a median INT8–FP32 cosine of 0.956, moves vectors by tens of degrees. Compressed storage adds reconstruction errors that audits must tolerate.

The authors recommend measuring exposure on the deployment's own corpus, recomputing and discarding shipped vectors where the device can afford it, and verifying codes with canonicalisation. Verification at 8 pairs per second costs the language model 23–31% of its decoding speed on the device CPU, so scheduling matters.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Median margins of 2.1–7.4 degrees make any tolerance's safety depend on corpus, model and storage format.

sections.body:
The conclusion restates that a tolerance-based binding concedes a share of queries set by the margin distribution. Margins are small in every corpus studied, so float-noise tolerances leave measurable exposure, INT8 calibration leaves 98–100% exposed, and compressed-store audits leave up to all queries exposed.

On a real FAISS index, a tolerance-passing attack ranked the attacker's document first for a quarter of targets. On the device, a comparable attack lowered correct answers from 0.75 to 0.39.

The authors state that closing the gap requires discarding shipped vectors, exact verification on a bit-reproducible stack, or code-level verification with canonicalisation, which accepted every honest vector in the samples on three platforms and four compute backends. Code, data, the reference verifier and the protocol are released.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The gap can be closed by verifier-side recomputation, exact computation or code-level canonicalisation, not by tolerances.

sections.body:
Declarations state that generative AI assistants helped identify literature, cross-check bibliographic metadata and write scripts, and that the authors verified every reference and reviewed all code and results. Funding came from securagen.ai, with which the authors are affiliated; that company develops commercial software in the discussed areas.

Ethics approval and consent are not applicable. Code and data are in the GitHub repository securagenai/signed-but-steerable, archived as release v1.0.2. Generated answers were produced with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct under the Qwen Research License.

Author contributions name Georgios Feretzakis and Alexandros Papaspyridis.
